rationale: A wins because it gives the founder more structurally different stories, especially "Mindbody owns the software studios run on and the marketplace that fills their classes" as a platform-power angle. B is cleaner, but it throws that lane away by refusing "Mindbody's assistant sets up a conflict with its own ClassPass marketplace" instead of reframing it as a cautious ownership story. A has a few hot headlines that need cooling; B is safer, but safer is not the same as more useful.
gaps_in_A: "and it's adding AI to both" overclaims. The update says the assistant is on the studio-software side; it does not say ClassPass is getting AI or sharing data.

"treats 50,000 studios' booking calendars as one data set" may be true, but the update only says Mindbody powers booking for 50,000 studios and uses booking data. Aggregation across all calendars needs proof.
"boutique fitness startups promised" is an assumed competitive narrative. A correctly asks for a named competitor, but the headline is ahead of the evidence.
gaps_in_B: "Mindbody's assistant sets up a conflict with its own ClassPass marketplace" is rightly rejected as a claim, but B misses the better version: platform power and ownership concentration without alleging conflict.
"yield-management thinking arriving at Main Street wellness businesses" is dressed-up analysis from one launch. It needs more evidence or it becomes consultant fog.
"Next step: journalist-fit-check" is premature. The pilot methodology, named studio, and ClassPass boundary should be fact-checked before matching reporters.
The data angle and customer-story angle lean on the same unnamed pilot proof, so the set is less distinct than it thinks.
